# Higher-dimensional Blaschke section bodies need not satisfy planar containments

Two actual ordinary-body certificates show why the planar section-body containment mechanism does not extend by replacing surface-length addition with Blaschke addition. The first uses the sharp simplex and a minimal d+1 cap circuit. The second uses one fixed cube and its actual center halfcaps; its section body has unbounded diameter. Thus these are not the archived obstruction caused by aggregating different fibers.

The archive comparison is `candidate 4b6ce6cf06c8f669`. The new planar statement being tested is `candidate 915dc3adcfe3fcf0`. Only ordinary background was consulted: surface-area representation and Blaschke addition, and the Kneser--Suss inequality, in Sections 6 and 18.2 of [R. J. Gardner, The Brunn--Minkowski inequality](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/jaw/COURSES/520s/523/HO.523.20/Gardner.BullAMS.02.pdf). All bodies and cap calculations below are explicit.

## 1. The exact one-body bookkeeping

Let B be a positive d-body and let H_j be finitely many proper caps with probability weights theta_j. Assume the weighted ORIGINAL-boundary trace has normal marginal beta S_B. Define the positively oriented section measure

    R=sum_j theta_j |u_j| T_j delta_(-u_j/|u_j|),

where H_j={u_j.X>=c_j} and T_j is its proper section coarea. The elementary cap-boundary decomposition gives

    sum_j theta_j S_(B intersect H_j)=beta S_B+R.    (1)

All examples below have proper sections and no coincident positive-area body facets, so no supporting allocation is being suppressed. Their section means equal the actual deepest source, their continuous normals have a positive balance, and every cap has common mass beta|B|.

Let A be the weighted Blaschke cap aggregate with surface measure equal to the left side of (1). When R is the surface-area measure of a positive body J, (1) says, up to translation,

    A=beta^(1/(d-1)) B # J.                         (2)

The power is essential: S_(sB)=s^(d-1)S_B. The planar proof uses both the identity of Blaschke and Minkowski addition and containment of a Minkowski average of cap subsets in B. Neither implication remains available in dimension at least three.

The valid Kneser--Suss conclusions are

    |A|^((d-1)/d)>=beta |B|^((d-1)/d)+|J|^((d-1)/d),
    |A|^((d-1)/d)>=sum_j theta_j |B intersect H_j|^((d-1)/d).
                                                            (3)

Both are lower bounds on the same aggregate. They do not imply a translated containment of J or an upper bound on its diameter.

## 2. Sharp simplex caps already refute the reflected containment

Let B be a d-simplex with vertices v_0,...,v_d and barycentric coordinates lambda_i. Set N=d+1, r=d/N, and let g be its centroid. Take

    H_i={lambda_i>=1/N},   theta_i=1/N,
    beta=r^d=Gamma_d.                                (4)

Every cap is the homothetic copy

    B intersect H_i=(1/N)v_i+rB.

Thus every cap has volume beta|B| and full surface-area measure r^(d-1)S_B. Each section centroid is g: its fixed barycentric coordinate is 1/N and the other d section-centroid coordinates are r/d=1/N. The d+1 cap normals form a positive minimal full-rank circuit.

On an original facet opposite vertex k, the k-th cap contributes zero original-boundary area. Each of the other d caps cuts the fraction r^(d-1) of that facet. Therefore the weighted original-boundary normal marginal is

    [d/N]r^(d-1)S_B=beta S_B.

This is the actual sharp ordinary simplex certificate. Its full normal-dependent convex-potential stress is also supplied by the archived facet convex-order theorem `candidate 8e69e6820cd6ee00`; the present normal-area calculation does not assume that stronger theorem to determine A or J.

Equation (1) now gives exactly

    A=rB,
    R=[r^(d-1)/N]S_B,
    J=sB,  s=r N^(-1/(d-1)).                         (5)

The scale-correct higher-dimensional candidate for the planar reflected containment would be

    -J+q subset beta^(1/(d-1))B.                     (6)

It is FALSE for every d>=3. An elementary simplex fact is

    -sB+q subset tB for some q  iff  t>=d s.          (7)

For B=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d), inclusion of q and all q-s e_i requires q_i>=s and sum_i q_i<=t, hence t>=ds. Conversely q=(s,...,s) works when t>=ds. Affine equivalence gives the general statement.

Substituting (5) into the necessary condition for (6) reduces it to

    d<=d^(1/(d-1)),

which fails for d>=3. For d=2 it is equality, precisely the sharp planar triangle phenomenon. The literal planar coefficient beta in place of beta^(1/(d-1)) fails as well, since beta is smaller.

In dimension three the exact values are

    r=3/4, beta=27/64, s=3/8,
    minimum reflected containment scale d s=9/8,
    beta^(1/2)=3sqrt(3)/8<9/8.                       (8)

Kneser--Suss is an equality in BOTH lines of (3) for this example, because the caps and the two summands in (2) are homothetic. Thus the failed containment cannot be recovered by adding only those inequalities or their equality characterization.

## 3. A fixed cube gives unbounded section-body diameter

Now take B=[0,1]^d, d>=3, with center g=(1/2,...,1/2). Choose positive numbers w_1,...,w_d summing to one. For each axis i use the two caps

    H_i^-={X_i<=1/2}, H_i^+={X_i>=1/2},
    theta_i^-=theta_i^+=w_i/2.                       (9)

Every cap has volume 1/2. Reflection in g proves that every halfspace containing g captures at least 1/2, and a coordinate halfspace proves equality. If a point differs from g in coordinate i, a coordinate cap through it captures less than 1/2. Hence g is the unique ACTUAL global deepest point and beta=1/2.

Every coordinate section has area and coarea one and centroid g. Opposite normals cancel with equal positive weights. Away from the cutting planes, exactly one member of each pair captures a boundary point, so

    W=sum_i (w_i/2)(1_(H_i^-)+1_(H_i^+))=1/2

surface-a.e. Thus this example satisfies the full signed normal-dependent physical stress identically, not just a normal-marginal identity. It uses a probability mixture of d actual two-cap critical circuits; it does not claim a single minimal full-rank circuit. The simplex example in Section 2 already covers that separate requirement.

At each of the normals +/-e_i, the full cap aggregate and section measures have masses

    a_i=(1+w_i)/2,       r_i=w_i/2,                   (10)

respectively. To check a_i, cuts normal to axis i contribute full facet area one with total weight w_i; every other cut contributes half the old facet area with weight 1-w_i. The section formula gives r_i directly. Hence S_A=(1/2)S_B+S_J exactly.

An axis box with facet-area masses s_i at +/-e_i has volume and side lengths

    V=(product_i s_i)^(1/(d-1)),
    l_i=V/s_i.                                      (11)

The products of all lengths except l_i equal s_i, verifying (11) without any reconstruction assumption. These positive boxes are the required surface-area bodies A and J, up to translation.

Set w_d=t and w_i=(1-t)/(d-1) for i<d, with 0<t<1. Formula (11) gives the J side lengths

    l_i(J)=(t/2)^(1/(d-1)) for i<d,
    l_d(J)=[(1-t)/(2(d-1))]
                          (t/2)^(-(d-2)/(d-1)).      (12)

In particular l_d(J) tends to infinity as t decreases to zero, while B is fixed. Thus no dimension-only constant C_d can ensure a translated containment J subset C_d B under the actual cap, section and normal-stress hypotheses above. Reflection makes no difference for these centrally symmetric boxes.

The cap aggregate A itself also need not fit inside B. Its long side is

    l_d(A)=[(d-t)/(2(d-1))]
                          [(1+t)/2]^(-(d-2)/(d-1)).  (13)

At t=0 its limit is [d/(d-1)]2^(-1/(d-1))>1: raising to d-1 reduces this to (1+1/(d-1))^(d-1)>2, whose binomial expansion has first two terms equal to 2 and further positive terms for d>=3. Therefore l_d(A)>1 for all sufficiently small positive t. Every input cap is a subset of B, but their Blaschke probability aggregate has no translate contained in B.

## 4. A fixed exact three-dimensional certificate

For d=3 choose

    w_1=w_2=12/25, w_3=1/25.

Then the surface-area masses are

    (a_1,a_2,a_3)=(37/50,37/50,13/25),
    (r_1,r_2,r_3)=(6/25,6/25,1/50).

The side lengths are

    A: (sqrt(13)/5, sqrt(13)/5, 37/(10sqrt(13))),
    J: (sqrt(2)/10, sqrt(2)/10, 6sqrt(2)/5).          (14)

The squared third length of A is 1369/1300>1. The third length of J has square 72/25, exceeding both (1/2)^2 and (1/2) itself, so it fails both the literal planar and the scale-correct square-root containment coefficients. No numerical reconstruction or approximate criticality is involved.

The aggregate volumes are finite and perfectly compatible with (3):

    |A|=37sqrt(13)/250,   |J|=3sqrt(2)/125.

The general family (12) has |J| tending to zero while its diameter tends to infinity. This explains why a volume lower bound cannot repair the missing translated containment in this direction.

## 5. Precise stopping conclusion

The planar all-status construction remains valid in dimension two. These examples rule out its proposed direct higher-dimensional containment replacement, even at one actual ordinary deepest source with exact common cap mass and section means. They do not refute a different mixed-volume inequality retaining additional directional information, and they are not mixed-integer counterexamples.

Unlike the archived cross-fiber volume obstruction, the cube B never changes, and all caps are subsets of that same B. The obstruction is the nonlinear reconstruction of a body from its surface-area measure. Any successful higher-dimensional route must retain more than the surface-area identity and ordinary Kneser--Suss bounds.

The companion `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_blaschke_section_containment_obstructions_slab_recovery.py` checks the exact simplex scaling, the box reconstruction, all six-cap area weights, and the rational containment certificates. The limiting and all-halfspace claims are proved analytically above.
